case_info.scenario: A 55-year-old female patient with a history of hypercholesterolemia and anxiety was referred for progressive imbalance while walking and intense fear of falling for the past 14 years. The patient had become progressively disabled and had been using a wheelchair for 4 years prior to presentation. Neurological examination showed gaze-evoked horizontal nystagmus in both directions along with slow saccades and gaze restriction in both vertical and horizontal planes. There was ataxic dysarthria. Tone was normal in all 4 limbs but stretch reflexes were absent and plantar fascia were mute. Limb power was normal. Ataxia was seen on finger-to-nose and heel-knee-shin tests. Chorea was present in both legs. Ankle inversion with bilateral hammertoes was noted. Electromyography revealed sensory neuronopathy. On brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffuse cerebellar atrophy was noted along with T2 hyperintensities in bilateral middle cerebellar peduncles, cerebellar white matter, pons, and bilateral thalamus (Figure). Psychiatric treatment was commenced for her severe anxiety but did not relieve the fear of falling.
case_info.caption: Magnetic resonance brain images showing T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities.
case_info.explanation: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA; choice A) is one of the most common autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias, caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the frataxin(FXN)gene, with onset typically occurring in the second decade of life. Associated peripheral neuropathy, dorsal root ganglionopathy, and dorsal column involvement lead to areflexia with early loss of distal vibration sense. Oculomotor findings include fixation instability and frequent square-wave jerks, while gaze-evoked nystagmus is less common.1Common systemic manifestations include cardiomyopathy, diabetes, and musculoskeletal abnormalities like scoliosis, pes cavus, foot inversion, and hammertoes.2Late-onset cases commonly present with spastic ataxia with preserved or even brisk reflexes, without systemic manifestations.2Brain MRI in patients with FRDA shows spinal cord atrophy with preserved cerebellar volume.1This patient had sensory neuronopathy and skeletal deformities in the feet. However, disease onset was in the fourth decade of life with absent reflexes, prominent gaze evoked nystagmus, slow saccades, gaze palsy, and diffuse cerebellar atrophy on MRI. Test results for FRDA genetics were negative. Fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS; choice B) is an X-linked disease seen in premutation (55-200 CGG repeats) carriers of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. Late-onset (older than 50 years) intention/action tremor and cerebellar ataxia are the core clinical manifestations of FXTAS. Cognitive dysfunction (eg, frontal subcortical dementia with predominant executive dysfunction), psychiatric problems (eg, anxiety, depression, and social avoidance), and parkinsonism are commonly associated.3Slow vertical saccade and impaired vertical optokinetic nystagmus can give rise to progressive supranuclear palsy phenotype.4Sensory axonal neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction can precede the motor symptoms. Manifestations are generally mild in female individuals. However, migraine, thyroid dysfunction, and fibromyalgia are more common comorbidities in female carriers.5Bilateral T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities of the middle cerebellar peduncles (middle cerebellar peduncles sign), diffuse cortical-cerebellar atrophy, and hyperintensities involving periventricular, splenial, and pontocerebellar regions are classic radiological features of FXTAS.3,5This patient was female and had anxiety, cerebellar ataxia, slow saccades, and hyperintensities involving middle cerebellar peduncles and cerebellum. FXTAS genetic test results were negative. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC; choice C) is an autosomal recessive neurovisceral lysosomal lipid storage disorder caused by mutation in theNPC1orNPC2genes. Cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and chorea are common movement disorders in adult-onset NPC, along with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and predominant downgaze restriction.6The age at onset can vary from the perinatal period to adults older than 50 years. Visceral involvement in the form of hepatosplenomegaly commonly precedes neurological manifestations. Psychosis, behavioral symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction are common and can remain as an isolated presentation in adult-onset NPC for several years.6Seizure and cataplexy are more frequent in late-infantile and juvenile forms. Demyelinating peripheral neuropathy can be associated with childhood-onset forms but are rare in adult-onset NPC. Brain MRI is mostly normal or can show cerebellar, frontal, and midbrain atrophy with disease progression. This patient had generalized anxiety disorder and mild cognitive impairment. No history of seizure was noted. There was no organomegaly, and gaze palsy was not supranuclear. NPC genetic test results were negative for this patient. In a clinical setting of undiagnosed slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, mitochondrial etiology (choice D) should not be missed. Presence of ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, retinitis pigmentosa, and history of seizure aid in the diagnosis. Mitochondrial syndromic disorders that can present with cerebellar ataxia are summarized in theTable.7Among them, mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma (POLG)–mediated disorders are the most common cause of mitochondrial ataxia. Sensory predominant axonal neuropathy, areflexia, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia are the most commonly associated nonataxic features.8,9Dystonia, chorea, myoclonus, ptosis, myopathy, cognitive impairment, and seizures can be associated.10Brain MRI shows T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities predominantly involving cerebellar white matter, middle cerebellar peduncles, and thalamus, while brain stem and occipital frontal white matter involvement can also be seen.8IfPOLG-mediated ataxia is suspected clinically and radiologically, the most appropriate next step would be either direct sequence analysis of thePOLGgene or next-generation sequencing panel for ataxia wherePOLGis included. Mitochondrial genetic panel analysis for this patient revealed compound heterozygous pathogenic mutation in thePOLGgene (choice D), c.2243 G>C (p.W748S) in one allele and c.1399 G>A (p.A467T) in the other allele. This case highlights the value of screening for mitochondrial etiology when facing adult-onset slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia of unknown etiology.

[Persona]

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge

- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.

- You have examined the patient case.

- Keep your response under 5 sentences.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA; choice A) is one of the most common autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias, caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the frataxin(FXN)gene, with onset typically occurring in the second decade of life. Associated peripheral neuropathy, dorsal root ganglionopathy, and dorsal column involvement lead to areflexia with early loss of distal vibration sense. Oculomotor findings include fixation instability and frequent square-wave jerks, while gaze-evoked nystagmus is less common.1Common systemic manifestations include cardiomyopathy, diabetes, and musculoskeletal abnormalities like scoliosis, pes cavus, foot inversion, and hammertoes.2Late-onset cases commonly present with spastic ataxia with preserved or even brisk reflexes, without systemic manifestations.2Brain MRI in patients with FRDA shows spinal cord atrophy with preserved cerebellar volume.1This patient had sensory neuronopathy and skeletal deformities in the feet. However, disease onset was in the fourth decade of life with absent reflexes, prominent gaze evoked nystagmus, slow saccades, gaze palsy, and diffuse cerebellar atrophy on MRI. Test results for FRDA genetics were negative. Fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS; choice B) is an X-linked disease seen in premutation (55-200 CGG repeats) carriers of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. Late-onset (older than 50 years) intention/action tremor and cerebellar ataxia are the core clinical manifestations of FXTAS. Cognitive dysfunction (eg, frontal subcortical dementia with predominant executive dysfunction), psychiatric problems (eg, anxiety, depression, and social avoidance), and parkinsonism are commonly associated.3Slow vertical saccade and impaired vertical optokinetic nystagmus can give rise to progressive supranuclear palsy phenotype.4Sensory axonal neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction can precede the motor symptoms. Manifestations are generally mild in female individuals. However, migraine, thyroid dysfunction, and fibromyalgia are more common comorbidities in female carriers.5Bilateral T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities of the middle cerebellar peduncles (middle cerebellar peduncles sign), diffuse cortical-cerebellar atrophy, and hyperintensities involving periventricular, splenial, and pontocerebellar regions are classic radiological features of FXTAS.3,5This patient was female and had anxiety, cerebellar ataxia, slow saccades, and hyperintensities involving middle cerebellar peduncles and cerebellum. FXTAS genetic test results were negative. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC; choice C) is an autosomal recessive neurovisceral lysosomal lipid storage disorder caused by mutation in theNPC1orNPC2genes. Cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and chorea are common movement disorders in adult-onset NPC, along with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and predominant downgaze restriction.6The age at onset can vary from the perinatal period to adults older than 50 years. Visceral involvement in the form of hepatosplenomegaly commonly precedes neurological manifestations. Psychosis, behavioral symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction are common and can remain as an isolated presentation in adult-onset NPC for several years.6Seizure and cataplexy are more frequent in late-infantile and juvenile forms. Brain MRI is mostly normal or can show cerebellar, frontal, and midbrain atrophy with disease progression. This patient had generalized anxiety disorder and mild cognitive impairment. No history of seizure was noted. There was no organomegaly, and gaze palsy was not supranuclear. NPC genetic test results were negative for this patient. In a clinical setting of undiagnosed slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, mitochondrial etiology (choice D) should not be missed. Presence of ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, retinitis pigmentosa, and history of seizure aid in the diagnosis. Mitochondrial syndromic disorders that can present with cerebellar ataxia are summarized in theTable.7Among them, mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma (POLG)–mediated disorders are the most common cause of mitochondrial ataxia. Mitochondrial genetic panel analysis for this patient revealed compound heterozygous pathogenic mutation in thePOLGgene (choice D), c.2243 G>C (p.W748S) in one allele and c.1399 G>A (p.A467T) in the other allele. This case highlights the value of screening for mitochondrial etiology when facing adult-onset slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia of unknown etiology.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA; choice A) is one of the most common autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias, caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the frataxin(FXN)gene, with onset typically occurring in the second decade of life. Associated peripheral neuropathy, dorsal root ganglionopathy, and dorsal column involvement lead to areflexia with early loss of distal vibration sense. Oculomotor findings include fixation instability and frequent square-wave jerks, while gaze-evoked nystagmus is less common.1Common systemic manifestations include cardiomyopathy, diabetes, and musculoskeletal abnormalities like scoliosis, pes cavus, foot inversion, and hammertoes.2Late-onset cases commonly present with spastic ataxia with preserved or even brisk reflexes, without systemic manifestations.2Brain MRI in patients with FRDA shows spinal cord atrophy with preserved cerebellar volume.1This patient had sensory neuronopathy and skeletal deformities in the feet. However, disease onset was in the fourth decade of life with absent reflexes, prominent gaze evoked nystagmus, slow saccades, gaze palsy, and diffuse cerebellar atrophy on MRI. Test results for FRDA genetics were negative. Fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS; choice B) is an X-linked disease seen in premutation (55-200 CGG repeats) carriers of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. Late-onset (older than 50 years) intention/action tremor and cerebellar ataxia are the core clinical manifestations of FXTAS. Cognitive dysfunction (eg, frontal subcortical dementia with predominant executive dysfunction), psychiatric problems (eg, anxiety, depression, and social avoidance), and parkinsonism are commonly associated.3Slow vertical saccade and impaired vertical optokinetic nystagmus can give rise to progressive supranuclear palsy phenotype.4Sensory axonal neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction can precede the motor symptoms. Manifestations are generally mild in female individuals. However, migraine, thyroid dysfunction, and fibromyalgia are more common comorbidities in female carriers.5Bilateral T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities of the middle cerebellar peduncles (middle cerebellar peduncles sign), diffuse cortical-cerebellar atrophy, and hyperintensities involving periventricular, splenial, and pontocerebellar regions are classic radiological features of FXTAS.3,5This patient was female and had anxiety, cerebellar ataxia, slow saccades, and hyperintensities involving middle cerebellar peduncles and cerebellum. FXTAS genetic test results were negative. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC; choice C) is an autosomal recessive neurovisceral lysosomal lipid storage disorder caused by mutation in theNPC1orNPC2genes. Cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and chorea are common movement disorders in adult-onset NPC, along with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and predominant downgaze restriction.6The age at onset can vary from the perinatal period to adults older than 50 years. Visceral involvement in the form of hepatosplenomegaly commonly precedes neurological manifestations. Psychosis, behavioral symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction are common and can remain as an isolated presentation in adult-onset NPC for several years.6Seizure and cataplexy are more frequent in late-infantile and juvenile forms. Demyelinating peripheral neuropathy can be associated with childhood-onset forms but are rare in adult-onset NPC. Brain MRI is mostly normal or can show cerebellar, frontal, and midbrain atrophy with disease progression. This patient had generalized anxiety disorder and mild cognitive impairment. No history of seizure was noted. There was no organomegaly, and gaze palsy was not supranuclear. NPC genetic test results were negative for this patient. In a clinical setting of undiagnosed slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, mitochondrial etiology (choice D) should not be missed. Presence of ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, retinitis pigmentosa, and history of seizure aid in the diagnosis. Mitochondrial syndromic disorders that can present with cerebellar ataxia are summarized in theTable.7Among them, mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma (POLG)–mediated disorders are the most common cause of mitochondrial ataxia. Sensory predominant axonal neuropathy, areflexia, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia are the most commonly associated nonataxic features.8,9Dystonia, chorea, myoclonus, ptosis, myopathy, cognitive impairment, and seizures can be associated.10Brain MRI shows T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities predominantly involving cerebellar white matter, middle cerebellar peduncles, and thalamus, while brain stem and occipital frontal white matter involvement can also be seen.8IfPOLG-mediated ataxia is suspected clinically and radiologically, the most appropriate next step would be either direct sequence analysis of thePOLGgene or next-generation sequencing panel for ataxia wherePOLGis included. Mitochondrial genetic panel analysis for this patient revealed compound heterozygous pathogenic mutation in thePOLGgene (choice D), c.2243 G>C (p.W748S) in one allele and c.1399 G>A (p.A467T) in the other allele. This case highlights the value of screening for mitochondrial etiology when facing adult-onset slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia of unknown etiology.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."

case_info.explanation: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA; choice A) is one of the most common autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias, caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the frataxin(FXN)gene, with onset typically occurring in the second decade of life. Associated peripheral neuropathy, dorsal root ganglionopathy, and dorsal column involvement lead to areflexia with early loss of distal vibration sense. Oculomotor findings include fixation instability and frequent square-wave jerks, while gaze-evoked nystagmus is less common.1Common systemic manifestations include cardiomyopathy, diabetes, and musculoskeletal abnormalities like scoliosis, pes cavus, foot inversion, and hammertoes.2Late-onset cases commonly present with spastic ataxia with preserved or even brisk reflexes, without systemic manifestations.2Brain MRI in patients with FRDA shows spinal cord atrophy with preserved cerebellar volume.1This patient had sensory neuronopathy and skeletal deformities in the feet. However, disease onset was in the fourth decade of life with absent reflexes, prominent gaze evoked nystagmus, slow saccades, gaze palsy, and diffuse cerebellar atrophy on MRI. Test results for FRDA genetics were negative. Fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS; choice B) is an X-linked disease seen in premutation (55-200 CGG repeats) carriers of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. Late-onset (older than 50 years) intention/action tremor and cerebellar ataxia are the core clinical manifestations of FXTAS. Cognitive dysfunction (eg, frontal subcortical dementia with predominant executive dysfunction), psychiatric problems (eg, anxiety, depression, and social avoidance), and parkinsonism are commonly associated.3Slow vertical saccade and impaired vertical optokinetic nystagmus can give rise to progressive supranuclear palsy phenotype.4Sensory axonal neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction can precede the motor symptoms. Manifestations are generally mild in female individuals. However, migraine, thyroid dysfunction, and fibromyalgia are more common comorbidities in female carriers.5Bilateral T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities of the middle cerebellar peduncles (middle cerebellar peduncles sign), diffuse cortical-cerebellar atrophy, and hyperintensities involving periventricular, splenial, and pontocerebellar regions are classic radiological features of FXTAS.3,5This patient was female and had anxiety, cerebellar ataxia, slow saccades, and hyperintensities involving middle cerebellar peduncles and cerebellum. FXTAS genetic test results were negative. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC; choice C) is an autosomal recessive neurovisceral lysosomal lipid storage disorder caused by mutation in theNPC1orNPC2genes. Cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and chorea are common movement disorders in adult-onset NPC, along with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and predominant downgaze restriction.6The age at onset can vary from the perinatal period to adults older than 50 years. Visceral involvement in the form of hepatosplenomegaly commonly precedes neurological manifestations. Psychosis, behavioral symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction are common and can remain as an isolated presentation in adult-onset NPC for several years.6Seizure and cataplexy are more frequent in late-infantile and juvenile forms. Demyelinating peripheral neuropathy can be associated with childhood-onset forms but are rare in adult-onset NPC. Brain MRI is mostly normal or can show cerebellar, frontal, and midbrain atrophy with disease progression. This patient had generalized anxiety disorder and mild cognitive impairment. No history of seizure was noted. There was no organomegaly, and gaze palsy was not supranuclear. NPC genetic test results were negative for this patient. In a clinical setting of undiagnosed slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, mitochondrial etiology (choice D) should not be missed. Presence of ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, retinitis pigmentosa, and history of seizure aid in the diagnosis. Mitochondrial syndromic disorders that can present with cerebellar ataxia are summarized in theTable.7Among them, mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma (POLG)–mediated disorders are the most common cause of mitochondrial ataxia. Sensory predominant axonal neuropathy, areflexia, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia are the most commonly associated nonataxic features.8,9Dystonia, chorea, myoclonus, ptosis, myopathy, cognitive impairment, and seizures can be associated.10Brain MRI shows T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities predominantly involving cerebellar white matter, middle cerebellar peduncles, and thalamus, while brain stem and occipital frontal white matter involvement can also be seen.8IfPOLG-mediated ataxia is suspected clinically and radiologically, the most appropriate next step would be either direct sequence analysis of thePOLGgene or next-generation sequencing panel for ataxia wherePOLGis included. Mitochondrial genetic panel analysis for this patient revealed compound heterozygous pathogenic mutation in thePOLGgene (choice D), c.2243 G>C (p.W748S) in one allele and c.1399 G>A (p.A467T) in the other allele. This case highlights the value of screening for mitochondrial etiology when facing adult-onset slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia of unknown etiology.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA; choice A) is one of the most common autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias, caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the frataxin(FXN)gene, with onset typically occurring in the second decade of life. Associated peripheral neuropathy, dorsal root ganglionopathy, and dorsal column involvement lead to areflexia with early loss of distal vibration sense. Oculomotor findings include fixation instability and frequent square-wave jerks, while gaze-evoked nystagmus is less common.1Common systemic manifestations include cardiomyopathy, diabetes, and musculoskeletal abnormalities like scoliosis, pes cavus, foot inversion, and hammertoes.2Late-onset cases commonly present with spastic ataxia with preserved or even brisk reflexes, without systemic manifestations.2Brain MRI in patients with FRDA shows spinal cord atrophy with preserved cerebellar volume.1This patient had sensory neuronopathy and skeletal deformities in the feet. However, disease onset was in the fourth decade of life with absent reflexes, prominent gaze evoked nystagmus, slow saccades, gaze palsy, and diffuse cerebellar atrophy on MRI. Test results for FRDA genetics were negative. Fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS; choice B) is an X-linked disease seen in premutation (55-200 CGG repeats) carriers of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. Late-onset (older than 50 years) intention/action tremor and cerebellar ataxia are the core clinical manifestations of FXTAS. Cognitive dysfunction (eg, frontal subcortical dementia with predominant executive dysfunction), psychiatric problems (eg, anxiety, depression, and social avoidance), and parkinsonism are commonly associated.3Slow vertical saccade and impaired vertical optokinetic nystagmus can give rise to progressive supranuclear palsy phenotype.4Sensory axonal neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction can precede the motor symptoms. Manifestations are generally mild in female individuals. However, migraine, thyroid dysfunction, and fibromyalgia are more common comorbidities in female carriers.5Bilateral T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities of the middle cerebellar peduncles (middle cerebellar peduncles sign), diffuse cortical-cerebellar atrophy, and hyperintensities involving periventricular, splenial, and pontocerebellar regions are classic radiological features of FXTAS.3,5This patient was female and had anxiety, cerebellar ataxia, slow saccades, and hyperintensities involving middle cerebellar peduncles and cerebellum. FXTAS genetic test results were negative. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC; choice C) is an autosomal recessive neurovisceral lysosomal lipid storage disorder caused by mutation in theNPC1orNPC2genes. Cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and chorea are common movement disorders in adult-onset NPC, along with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and predominant downgaze restriction.6The age at onset can vary from the perinatal period to adults older than 50 years. Visceral involvement in the form of hepatosplenomegaly commonly precedes neurological manifestations. Psychosis, behavioral symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction are common and can remain as an isolated presentation in adult-onset NPC for several years.6Seizure and cataplexy are more frequent in late-infantile and juvenile forms. Demyelinating peripheral neuropathy can be associated with childhood-onset forms but are rare in adult-onset NPC. Brain MRI is mostly normal or can show cerebellar, frontal, and midbrain atrophy with disease progression. This patient had generalized anxiety disorder and mild cognitive impairment. No history of seizure was noted. There was no organomegaly, and gaze palsy was not supranuclear. NPC genetic test results were negative for this patient. In a clinical setting of undiagnosed slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, mitochondrial etiology (choice D) should not be missed. Presence of ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, retinitis pigmentosa, and history of seizure aid in the diagnosis. Mitochondrial syndromic disorders that can present with cerebellar ataxia are summarized in theTable.7Among them, mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma (POLG)–mediated disorders are the most common cause of mitochondrial ataxia. Sensory predominant axonal neuropathy, areflexia, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia are the most commonly associated nonataxic features.8,9Dystonia, chorea, myoclonus, ptosis, myopathy, cognitive impairment, and seizures can be associated.10Brain MRI shows T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities predominantly involving cerebellar white matter, middle cerebellar peduncles, and thalamus, while brain stem and occipital frontal white matter involvement can also be seen.8IfPOLG-mediated ataxia is suspected clinically and radiologically, the most appropriate next step would be either direct sequence analysis of thePOLGgene or next-generation sequencing panel for ataxia wherePOLGis included. Mitochondrial genetic panel analysis for this patient revealed compound heterozygous pathogenic mutation in thePOLGgene (choice D), c.2243 G>C (p.W748S) in one allele and c.1399 G>A (p.A467T) in the other allele. This case highlights the value of screening for mitochondrial etiology when facing adult-onset slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia of unknown etiology.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 55-year-old female patient with a history of hypercholesterolemia and anxiety was referred for progressive imbalance while walking and intense fear of falling for the past 14 years. The patient had become progressively disabled and had been using a wheelchair for 4 years prior to presentation. Neurological examination showed gaze-evoked horizontal nystagmus in both directions along with slow saccades and gaze restriction in both vertical and horizontal planes. There was ataxic dysarthria. Tone was normal in all 4 limbs but stretch reflexes were absent and plantar fascia were mute. Limb power was normal. Ataxia was seen on finger-to-nose and heel-knee-shin tests. Chorea was present in both legs. Ankle inversion with bilateral hammertoes was noted. Electromyography revealed sensory neuronopathy. On brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffuse cerebellar atrophy was noted along with T2 hyperintensities in bilateral middle cerebellar peduncles, cerebellar white matter, pons, and bilateral thalamus (Figure). Psychiatric treatment was commenced for her severe anxiety but did not relieve the fear of falling.

case_info.scenario: A 55-year-old female patient with a history of hypercholesterolemia and anxiety was referred for progressive imbalance while walking and intense fear of falling for the past 14 years. The patient had become progressively disabled and had been using a wheelchair for 4 years prior to presentation. Neurological examination showed gaze-evoked horizontal nystagmus in both directions along with slow saccades and gaze restriction in both vertical and horizontal planes. There was ataxic dysarthria. Tone was normal in all 4 limbs but stretch reflexes were absent and plantar fascia were mute. Limb power was normal. Ataxia was seen on finger-to-nose and heel-knee-shin tests. Chorea was present in both legs. Ankle inversion with bilateral hammertoes was noted. Electromyography revealed sensory neuronopathy. On brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffuse cerebellar atrophy was noted along with T2 hyperintensities in bilateral middle cerebellar peduncles, cerebellar white matter, pons, and bilateral thalamus (Figure).
